stories.title: Samuel Eto’o urges support for embattled FIFA President Gianni Infantino
stories.summary: Former star striker, now head of Cameroon’s football association, backs Infantino despite mounting pressure on him to resign. Former Cameroon star Samuel Eto’o has thrown his support behind beleaguered FIFA President Gianni Infantino, saying he “hasn’t done anything wrong” despite facing mounting pressure to step down over a controversial World Cup selloff plan. Infantino has come under intense scrutiny since the collapse of a proposal to secure private investment in FIFA tournaments, including the World Cup. UEFA, which oversees European football, has threatened a boycott of FIFA competitions, with several continental and national federations also withdrawing their support for Infantino. However, Eto’o, president of the Cameroonian Football Federation, dismissed criticism of Infantino’s leadership, suggesting the backlash was driven largely by political manoeuvring ahead of FIFA’s presidential election next year. “I don’t think that President Gianni Infantino has done anything wrong,” the former Barcelona, Inter Milan and Chelsea striker told CNN. “I think the timing of all of that is because there’s an election coming out.” Infantino’s plan, which would reportedly have distributed substantial funding to FIFA’s 211 member associations, faced strong opposition from several confederations and was ultimately abandoned. The FIFA president remains under pressure, with the possibility of a no-confidence vote being triggered. UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), and the Confederation of North, Central American and Caribbean Association Football (CONCACAF) have all voiced concerns over FIFA’s direction in recent weeks. But the Confederation of African Football (CAF) earlier this month “unanimously reconfirmed its support” for Infantino, and Eto’o’s backing is aligned with that position. “President Gianni Infantino has changed football,” said Eto’o, urging fellow African countries to support the Swiss official.

stories.summary: The French government said on Monday it would press ahead with a ban on mobile phones in high schools from next month, but trade unions warned that the measure might be hard to implement quickly. stories.title: West turns Ukraine into 'frontier country' making money on war — economist
stories.summary: Oleg Pendzin noted that Ukraine exists solely through financial injections, aid, mercenaries, and weaponry
article_sentences: MOSCOW, August 24.

The West has transformed Ukraine into a "frontier nation," whose sole purpose appears to be waging war while relying heavily on foreign aid, according to Oleg Pendzin, executive director of the Ukrainian Economic Discussion Club, who was speaking in an interview with the UNIAN news agency.
"From day one of the conflict, we've been fighting on borrowed money," Pendzin stated.
"The socio-political climate surrounding us is causing significant concerns among our European partners regarding their own futures.
Essentially, they are buying off Ukrainian blood."
Pendzin pointed out that Europe seems intent on shifting the entire burden of the conflict onto Ukrainian shoulders by funneling money and weapons into the country.
He described Ukraine as a "frontier country" that exists solely through financial injections, aid, mercenaries, and weaponry - serving as a shield rather than an independent nation.
"Ukraine cannot survive solely on its own resources at this point," he emphasized.
"Imagine if we didn't have access to the recent 90 billion euros from the EU lending program - our entire social system would collapse instantly.
There would be no social assistance, no salaries for public sector workers, no aid for the impoverished, no pensions."
For several years, Ukraine's budget has been plagued by a record deficit.
Domestic revenues no longer fully cover even military expenses, with Western aid filling the gap for most other expenditures.

stories.title: Malian PM's visit to Algeria underlines need for mutual security goals
stories.summary: The acting head of the Malian government, General Abdoulaye Maiga has begun a two-day visit to Algeria. It comes amid a thaw after months of tension. RFI spoke to Bakary Sambe, the Director of the Timbuktu Institute about the security situation and what the countries hope to gain from the meeting.
